QRILC — Quantile Regression for Left-Censored data

method = qrilc
MNAR-aware imputation drawn from a truncated log-normal (Lazar 2016, <em>J Proteome Res</em> 15:1116). Missing cells are sampled from the lower tail estimated per-feature.

Pre-imputation missingness heatmap (top 600 features)
diagnostic — input state
Dark = detected, white = missing. Rows ranked by missing %. Columns grouped by injection type (blank / QC / biological / dilution). Whole-sample white stripes flag a failed injection; whole-feature white bands are common for group-private metabolites.
↗ open interactive ⬇ PNG
Per-feature missing-rate distribution
diagnostic — input state
How concentrated is the missingness? A right-leaning distribution (many features mostly-missing) means the matrix is sparse and MNAR-imputation accuracy matters more.
↗ open interactive ⬇ PNG
Imputed vs observed distribution (log10 scale)
diagnostic — Wei et al. 2018 (log10 view)
Cross-feature view of where imputed values land relative to the observed signal. LC-MS abundances span 4–6 orders of magnitude so log10 is required for readability — on linear axes both curves collapse to a single spike near zero. Half-min and QRILC are <em>per-feature</em> LOD surrogates: for each feature, imputed values are smaller than that feature's own observed minimum. Across the whole feature set, the imputed distribution should sit clearly to the left of the bulk of the observed distribution — broad overlap (rather than a left-shifted bump) would indicate a MAR-style estimator instead of LOD-surrogate behaviour.
↗ open interactive ⬇ PNG
Per-feature property test (imputed / observed min)
per-feature LOD-surrogate test
Per-feature LOD-surrogate sanity check. For a textbook half-min imputer (<code>factor=0.5</code>) every imputed cell equals half its own feature's smallest observed value, so the histogram is a single bar at 0.5. QRILC samples from a left-truncated normal, so its bars spread below 1 with no single mode. Mass above 1 (right of the dotted line) means some imputed value exceeded that feature's observed minimum — a red flag for MNAR methods, expected for kNN / missForest under MAR-like patterns.
↗ open interactive ⬇ PNG
Per-sample imputed-cell count
diagnostic — operator-level QA
Bars stacked by injection type. Even spread = healthy. Spikes on a single biological sample suggest a bad injection; spikes on QCs are unusual and worth investigating.

QC-RSC drift correction (cubic-spline anchored on QC injections)

method = qc_rsc
Per-feature cubic spline through QC intensities at their run-order positions, evaluated at every sample's position to estimate drift, then divided out (Kirwan 2013, <em>Analyst</em> 138:5337). The transparent gold standard for single-batch acquisitions.

mQACC metric panel
D-ratio · PMSD · QC-CV · silhouette (Broadhurst 2018, Kirwan 2013)
Headline drift-quality metrics. Lower is better for D-ratio (Broadhurst 2018: &lt; 0.5 acceptable, &lt; 0.4 good), PMSD, and median QC-CV. Higher is better for biological silhouette — if it drops by &gt; 5 % the correction is suspected of erasing biology (De Livera 2015 guardrail).

Eight features sampled across the QC-CV percentile range. Dotted line is pre-correction, solid is post-correction. Vertical grey hairlines mark QC injection positions. Successful correction = the post-trace is flat across the run; pre-trace shows a slope or curve.

D-ratio distribution (Broadhurst 2018)
The bulk of features should shift left (lower D-ratio) post-correction. Mass to the right of the 0.5 threshold = features still drift-dominated. Top 1 % truncated for readability.

Per-feature coefficient of variation across the QC pool. Mass below 30 % = drift-corrected features that are also analytically reproducible (the two-pass mQACC criterion). Tail clipped to 200 % for readability.

PQN — Probabilistic Quotient Normalization

method = pqn
Per-sample factor = median of per-feature quotients against a reference spectrum (Dieterle 2006, <em>Anal Chem</em> 78:4281). The robust default for clinical and discovery metabolomics; the median makes the estimate insensitive to a few differentially-expressed features.

Generalized logarithm (glog) transformation

method = glog
Generalized logarithm: ``y = log(x + sqrt(x² + λ))`` (Parsons 2007). Linearises the noise floor of low-abundance features more aggressively than log2 — useful when zero-inflated or imputed LOD values dominate.

Headline metric panel
van den Berg 2006 transformation framework
Heteroscedasticity slope: closer to 0 = better variance stabilisation (van den Berg 2006). Mean |skewness|: lower = more symmetric distributions. KS-normal fraction: higher = more features look log-normal.

Heteroscedasticity (before)
heteroscedasticity slope (van den Berg 2006)
Each point = one feature. A slope near 1 means SD scales with mean — the classical right-skewed pattern that needs log.

Heteroscedasticity (after)
heteroscedasticity slope (van den Berg 2006)
Slope should drop towards 0 — variance stabilised across the dynamic range. Residual slope &gt; 0.3 = variance still scales with mean.

Per-feature skewness violin
skewness distribution (Parsons 2007)
Symmetric distributions cluster around 0. LC-MS intensities are right-skewed pre-log (median &gt; 1, often 3–10); post-log they should fall to ≤ 1.

Per-feature mean intensity — before
distribution shape (raw scale)
log10 of the raw per-feature mean. LC-MS abundances are approximately log-normal; expect a roughly bell-shaped distribution centred on the typical log-abundance, with the spread reflecting the dynamic range of the experiment.

Per-feature mean intensity — after
distribution shape (transformed)
Distribution after the chosen transformation. For log2 the x-axis is signed log2-units; the distribution should look more symmetric than its raw counterpart and is bounded above by ~log2(max raw intensity).

Pareto scaling — (x − mean) / √SD per feature

method = pareto
Per-feature centring with √SD denominator (van den Berg 2006, <em>BMC Genomics</em> 7:142). Less aggressive than auto-scale, more informative than mean-only centring. The default for multivariate metabolomics.
per-feature mean (after) — median |·|
0.0
should be ≈ 0 — verifies centring
per-feature SD (after) — median
0.8088
for Pareto, ≈ sqrt(median SD_before)
per-feature SD (before) — median
0.6541
n_constant_features
0features
features with SD = 0 in input — bypassed (no scaling applied)
Mean-zero verification
centring sanity check
All mass should sit in a tight bar centred on 0. Spread away from 0 = centring bug. Constant features (SD = 0) are passed through unchanged in Pareto and may sit off-zero — these are flagged separately.
↗ open interactive ⬇ PNG
Per-feature SD distribution
SD distribution (van den Berg 2006)
Pareto compresses the SD distribution: SD_after ≈ sqrt(SD_before). On log10 the &quot;after&quot; curve should sit at half the abscissa of the &quot;before&quot; curve and have smaller spread.
↗ open interactive ⬇ PNG
Pareto identity check
Pareto algebraic identity
If Pareto is correctly applied, points fall on the y = x line. Deviation from y = x = numerical bug or unexpected scaling. Constant features (sqrt(SD_before) = 0) excluded.

SIMCA outlier diagnostic — Hotelling T² + DModX

method = simca_t2_dmodx
Per-sample outlier flagging from PCA scores (T²) and residuals (DModX). Samples are <em>flagged for review</em>, never auto-removed — the user decides whether to add a flagged sample to <code>parse.exclude_samples</code> and rerun the pipeline. Includes a class-ellipse PCA (Kirwan 2013) showing biology + QC structure.

T² × DModX outlier scatter
Hotelling T² (Wold 1976) · DModX (Eriksson 2006)
Biological samples (circles, coloured by cell line) flagged by the SIMCA model. QC samples (grey diamonds) are projected onto the same biological-fit model as a sanity check — they should cluster tightly in the lower-left quadrant. Critical-value lines split the plane: <em>lower-left</em> = normal; <em>lower-right</em> = biological extreme (high T², shape fits); <em>upper-left</em> = technical artifact (DModX high, position OK); <em>upper-right</em> = comprehensive outlier. Flagged biological samples are labelled with their sample id.
↗ open interactive ⬇ PNG
PCA scores with class + QC ellipses
Kirwan 2013 class-ellipse PCA
PC1 × PC2 with one 95 % confidence ellipse per cell line and one for the QC pool. The QC ellipse should be small and central — tight QCs confirm the upstream drift correction and normalisation did their job. Cell-line ellipses should be reasonably separated and similar in size — confirms biology survived preprocessing. Flagged outlier samples (from the T² × DModX panel above) carry their sample id as a label.
↗ open interactive ⬇ PNG
Hotelling's T² per sample
Hotelling T² (Eriksson 2006)
Per-sample T² with the dashed critical line. Bars exceeding the line are flagged in the scatter above; the colour is the cell line. QC bars (grey) are projections onto the biological-fit model — they should sit well below the threshold.
↗ open interactive ⬇ PNG
DModX per sample
DModX (Eriksson 2006)
Per-sample DModX (out-of-model distance). Bars above the critical line indicate samples whose shape isn't well explained by the PC model — usually a technical issue. QC DModX values (grey) should be small (QCs reconstruct well from the biological PC model).

Univariate statistics — one-way ANOVA + BH-FDR + η² + per-pair log2 FC + Tukey HSD

method = anova_bh_eta_tukey
Per-feature one-way ANOVA across the cell-line groups followed by Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction (q-value), η² effect size (Cohen 1988), per-pair log2 fold-change + Cohen's d, and Tukey HSD post-hoc for ANOVA-significant features. Every feature's significance gets a magnitude companion (η² for the omnibus, log2 FC + Cohen's d for each contrast) so the shortlist can filter on biological meaning, not just p-value.

P-value histogram (uniform null expected under no signal)
p-value distribution (Benjamini & Hochberg 1995)
Distribution of raw ANOVA p-values across all features. Under the global null (no real biology) p-values are uniform — every bar should sit near the dotted reference line. Excess mass near zero = real signal. The taller the spike at the lowest bin, the more discoveries BH-FDR will accept.
↗ open interactive ⬇ PNG
η² distribution with Cohen's small/medium/large reference lines
η² (Cohen 1988)
Per-feature effect size from the one-way ANOVA. Cohen's convention: η² ≥ 0.01 = small, ≥ 0.06 = medium, ≥ 0.14 = large. Features in the right tail carry meaningful biological magnitude; features with significant p but low η² are real but marginal — filter them out at the shortlist stage.
↗ open interactive ⬇ PNG
Per-pair volcano plots
ANOVA q + per-pair log2 FC
One subplot per cell-line pair. x = pair-specific log2 FC (mean_A − mean_B on log scale), y = −log10(ANOVA q-value) shared across panels (the omnibus test isn't pair-specific). Threshold lines: q = 0.05 (orange dashed) and |log2 FC| = 1 (grey dotted). Points in the upper-outer corners are the shortlist candidates.
↗ open interactive ⬇ PNG
Top-30 features by −log10(q), coloured by η²
top-N significance × effect-size view
The single most useful overview when triaging discoveries. Bars descend by ANOVA −log10(q); colour saturates with η² so a tall, dark bar is both significant AND large-effect. Shortlist candidates dominate the left side of this plot.
↗ open interactive ⬇ PNG
Tukey post-hoc heatmap
Tukey HSD (Tukey 1953)
Per-pair fraction of features whose Tukey HSD post-hoc test is significant. In <code>auto</code> mode (default) Tukey is computed only for ANOVA-significant features, so this matrix asks: <em>among the features ANOVA flagged, which contrasts drive that signal?</em> Hotter cells = more contrasts within that pair.

Multivariate — PLS-DA (Geladi & Kowalski 1986)

method = plsda
Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis used as a feature-importance generator (NOT a classifier). Per-feature VIP, β coefficients per class, permutation importance, bootstrap stability (Nogueira 2018) and label-shuffle p-values (Westerhuis 2008). VIP ≥ 1 + stability ≥ 0.8 + perm p &lt; 0.05 is the canonical mQACC shortlist gate.

PLS-DA score plot with class ellipses
PLS-DA scores (Wold 1973)
Sample projections onto the first two PLS components. Tight non-overlapping ellipses = strong class separation; overlapping ellipses = the classes are not well discriminated by this model. QC samples (grey diamonds) are projected onto the same model and should sit near the centroid — they're a pooled mixture of biology so they shouldn't favour any class.
↗ open interactive ⬇ PNG
β-coefficient heatmap
PLS β coefficients (Wold 1995)
Sign and magnitude of each top-N feature's contribution to every class. Red = positive (feature high in this class), blue = negative (feature low). A feature with one strong red column and weak blues is a clean class-private biomarker.

Multivariate — sPLS-DA (sparse PLS-DA, Lê Cao 2011)

method = splsda
Sparse Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis: hard-sparsity NIPALS that keeps only the top-K weights per component, zeroing the rest. Returns an explicit <code>selected</code> mask — biomarkers carry that flag through the rest of the report. Avoids the &quot;everything looks important&quot; problem of vanilla PLS-DA on small N.

Multivariate — Random Forest (Breiman 2001)

method = rf
Random Forest classifier used as a feature-importance generator. Reports BOTH Gini importance (default sklearn) AND permutation importance (Strobl 2007 — less biased toward high-cardinality features). Real biomarkers should rank high in BOTH — the Gini vs perm scatter makes this comparison visible.

Gini vs permutation importance (Strobl 2007)
Gini × perm importance (Strobl 2007)
Real biomarkers should cluster on the diagonal (high Gini AND high perm). Off-diagonal points: features with high Gini but low perm importance are the classical Gini-bias false positives (high cardinality / many split points). Trust the perm-importance ranking when they disagree.

OOB-score trajectory (saturation diagnostic)
RF OOB trajectory
Out-of-bag accuracy as the forest grows. The curve should plateau before <code>n_estimators</code> — earlier saturation means more trees would just inflate runtime. Confirms the small-N rule <code>n_estimators = max(100, n_samples × 10)</code>.

Path summary — attrition, runtime, cross-method consensus

method = path_summary
End-of-path roll-up. Shows feature attrition through the pipeline, runtime breakdown, and the cross-method overlap of biomarker shortlists computed at standard thresholds. Consensus across methods (≥ 2 / 3+) is the multiverse design's strongest defensible signal (Steegen 2016).

Feature attrition waterfall
cumulative attrition
Bar height = features remaining after each stage. The biomarker-discovery shape: steep early drops at presence / blank filters, gentler attrition through variance-aware stages, then a final shortlist cliff. Hover for the per-step delta.
↗ open interactive ⬇ PNG
Cross-method shortlist Jaccard heatmap
pairwise Jaccard (Nogueira 2018)
Pairwise Jaccard = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B| of method-specific shortlists. High values along a row = that method agrees with the others; isolated low cells = method-specific discoveries that need extra justification before going on the consensus shortlist.
↗ open interactive ⬇ PNG
Consensus agreement bar
multiverse consensus tiers
Cleaner alternative to a Venn diagram: how many features are flagged by exactly 1, 2, 3, … methods? Tier-1 consensus = features in ≥ 3 / k methods (Steegen 2016).
↗ open interactive ⬇ PNG
Per-stage runtime breakdown
runtime breakdown
Wall-clock seconds per pipeline stage. Bootstrap and permutation loops dominate multivariate methods; filtering and per-feature stats are typically &lt; 1 s each.
